questions.question: Define a longitudinal profile, and explain how you would identify the graded profile when an exam sketch shows two versions side by side.
questions.expected_answer: A longitudinal profile is a side view of a river from its source to its mouth. The graded profile is the smooth, concave curve — steep near the source, flattening gently to the mouth — with no waterfalls, steps or interruptions, because erosion and deposition are in balance along its length. The ungraded profile shows irregularities such as a waterfall over resistant rock or a dam creating a temporary base level, while the sea forms the permanent base level neither profile can cut below.

questions.question: Explain why the outer bank of a meander is steep while the inner bank is gentle, naming both banks.
questions.expected_answer: Water on the outside of the bend travels the longer path and therefore moves fastest, so it erodes and undercuts the bank, forming the steep undercut slope. Water on the inside travels the short path slowly, so it cannot carry its load and deposits sand and gravel there, building the gentle slip-off slope. Fast water erodes; slow water deposits — the speed difference explains both banks.

questions.question: In a paragraph, explain how an oxbow lake is formed and what it eventually becomes.
questions.expected_answer: Continuous erosion attacks the outer banks of both limbs of the meander while deposition builds the inner banks, so the meander neck narrows from both sides. During a flood the river has enough energy to break through the narrowed neck, and the straighter, faster shortcut becomes the main channel. Deposition then seals both ends of the abandoned loop, cutting it off as a horseshoe-shaped oxbow lake. Cut off from the flow, the lake gradually evaporates, silts up and is overgrown until only a curved meander scar remains on the floodplain.
